uses.text: Laboratory, analytical and specialty gases are the largest use (22 %), then inert atmospheres for making chips and optical fibre (17 %).
Liquid helium cools the superconducting magnets of MRI scanners (15 %).
Lifts balloons and airships (17 %); also used in welding (8 %) and in breathing gas for diving (5 %).
Finds leaks in vacuum and pressure equipment (5 %); helium-3 is used in neutron detectors and quantum-computing research.

sectors.text: Helium goes into data centres (storage and servers), according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.

hazardStatements.text: Contains gas under pressure; may explode if heated
Contains refrigerated gas; may cause cryogenic burns or injury

hazards.note: Aggregated by PubChem from 491 reports by companies to the ECHA C&L Inventory; the percentage after a statement is the share of reports that give it. 0.4 % of the reports (2 of 491) say helium does not meet the GHS hazard criteria.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

origin.note: Fig. 39 cannot be read for helium: its box is full to the top, and the paper says the coloured areas include helium that stars merely returned to space. Most helium was made in the Big Bang, but the figure gives no split we can quote.

bonding.note: Single atoms; helium stays liquid down to absolute zero unless it is put under pressure.

water.text: No reaction with water; very slightly soluble in it.

acids.text: Inert: forms no stable compounds under ordinary conditions.

compounds.note: No stable neutral compound is known; the HeH⁺ ion and Na₂He (made only at very high pressure) are the exceptions.

siHistory.text: The He–Ne laser (633 nm, helium and neon) is a recommended radiation for realizing the metre.

biology.note: Not known to be essential for plants or for humans.

history.nameOrigin: From the Greek helios, 'Sun', because it was first seen as an unexplained yellow line in the solar spectrum.
history.note: Janssen recorded the line during the solar eclipse of August 1868 (the map dot is his observing site) and Lockyer argued it came from an unknown element. Ramsay found the gas on Earth in the uranium mineral cleveite in 1895; Cleve and Langlet found it there independently.

prose.text: Helium is a noble gas, the second lightest element and the second most common in the universe; on Earth it is collected from natural gas, where it has gathered after being released as alpha particles by uranium and thorium decaying in rocks. It was first spotted in 1868 as a yellow line near 587.6 nm in the light of the Sun, long before anyone found it on Earth. Its two electrons fill the 1s shell (ground term ¹S₀), giving helium the highest first ionisation energy of any element, about 2372 kJ/mol, so it forms no stable compounds under ordinary conditions.
